g: fatḥa (فَتْحَة), indicates a short /a/ or its cognates, indicates a long /aː/ if followed by an ا (ʔalif).
ḍamma – ضَمَّة (ḍamma) – indicates a short /u/ or its cognates, indicates a long /uː/ if followed by a و (w).
Forms the nominative determinative inflections of nouns.
Forms the indicative mood of present-tense verbs.
kasra (كسرَة), indicates a short /i/ or its cognates, indicates a long /iː/ if followed by a ي (y).
shadda (شَدَّة (šadda)), indicates a geminate (long, double) consonant.
superscript alif, dagger alif (أَلِف خَنْجَرِيَّة (ʔalif ḵanjariyya)), indicates a long /aː/ where ا (ʔalif) is normally not written.

fatḥa tanwīn (فتحَة تنوين) or fatḥatān (فتحتان), a nunation (tanwīn (تنوين)) of the vowel a (ـَ - fatḥa), indicating the accusative case in Classical Arabic, usually used in combination with ا (ʔalif) - (ـًا), unless it's ة (ةً) or ء (ʔ) (ءً). In a non-pausal formal situation it's pronounced as "-an".

ḍamma tanwīn (ضَمَّة تَنْوِين) or ḍammatān (ضَمَّتَان), a nunation (tanwīn (تَنْوِين)) of the vowel u (ـُ - ḍamma), indicating the nominative case in Classical Arabic. In a non-pausal formal situation it's pronounced as "-un". In dialects, relaxed (less formal) Arabic, or in pausa, the pronunciation is either shortened to "-u" or ignored altogether, even when written.

kasra tanwīn (كَسْرَة تَنْوِين) or kasratān (كَسْرَتَان), a nunation (tanwīn (تَنْوِين)) of the vowel i (ـِ - kasra), indicating the genitive case in Classical Arabic. In a non-pausal formal situation it's pronounced as "-in". In dialects, relaxed (less formal) Arabic or in pausa, the pronunciation is either shorted to "-i" or ignored altogether, even when written.

Over an alif (آ (ʾā) "alif maddah"), it indicates glottal stop, /ʔ/, followed by a long /aː/. The diacritic is not used separately, only over alif. Alif maddah can appear in the beginning: آسِف (ʾāsif) or in the middle of a word: قُرْآن (qurʾān).

A marking used in Qur'anic scripture to indicate that while a pause can be made at the point it appears in the text, it is recommended that one recite the scripture without a pause. Semantically, it is more or less equivalent to the Qur'anic symbol used in the Arab world, ﷰ. This character is also comparable to small high ط (which is used in Iran as roughly equivalent to ﷱ).
Diacritic which denotes imala.
In the Qur'an, it indicates extra long vowel and can appear over any long vowel.
Indicates the absence of a vowel after a consonant.
used to indicate that a letter is silent
indicates that the letter is pronounced only when one pauses on the word during recitation, but if one continues reading without pausing, the letter is not pronounced.
A small pause without taking a breath whilst reading the Holy Qur'an
Quran 2:2

maddeler.t: From اَلْوَصْلُ أَوْلَى (al-waṣlu ʔawlā, “continuing is preferred”).
g: A mark in the Qur'an indicating an optional pause.

maddeler.t: From اَلْوَقْفُ أَوْلَى (al-waqfu ʔawlā, “pausing is preferred”).
g: A marking used in Quranic scripture to denote a pause, almost always at the end of a sentence.
A diacritic used in the Qur'an to indicate a required pause

maddeler.t: From لَا تَقِفْ (lā taqif, “Do not pause”).
g: A diacritic used in the Qur'an to indicate that the reader should NOT pause.
Arabic Puncuation mark. It marks that you COULD read it nonstop, but you don't have to. If you read it nonstop then you have to pronounce that letter
